title: Fold a collapsible crate flat for storage
instruction: Fold the empty crate flat for storage, and finish with both arms back where they started.
context: Collapsible plastic crates are an everyday household item: people carry shopping in them from the car, keep them in the boot, use them for laundry, picnics, garden produce and home storage, and fold them flat between uses. They sell for a few dollars or pounds at warehouse clubs, supermarkets and DIY stores (for example Costco's 12-gallon InstaCrate, the 32 L folding crates at Wickes and B&Q, and Mount-It's folding trunk crate at Target). Many fold the way this one does; one maker's instructions read "Using your thumbs, press buttons on the short ends and fold the flaps down", then "Fold the long sides in". Anyone who has used one recognises the job at a glance. For a robot it is hard because two sprung catches 20 cm apart must be held open at the same time against their springs, the light crate must not be shoved across the table while doing it, and the walls must go down in the order the hardware allows: both end walls first, then the long walls on top.
setup: Left and right are the robot's; positions in metres from the midpoint between the two arm bases (61 cm apart), x forward, y to the robot's left, heights above the table top (75 cm high). One object: an empty green folding crate, built to the README's drawings, STL files and parts list: 400 x 300 mm, 174 mm tall to its rails (the four catch housings 176 mm), 1.03 kg, standing up on the table centred at (0.23, 0.00) with its 400 mm length along x, so one short end wall faces the robot and the other faces away. Base: 6 mm floor and 10 mm rims of fluted polypropylene sheet, the long-side rims 68 mm tall and the end rims 48 mm, 0.413 kg with its printed PETG brackets. Walls: 10 mm fluted polypropylene panels, each on two hinges (4 mm steel pins) at the inner top edge of its rim, folding inward between an upright stop and a flat stop. The two end walls (270 x 126 mm, 0.146 kg each) have a 120 x 36 mm handhold under a 16 mm round PETG top rail; the two long walls (400 x 106 mm, 0.153 kg each) have a 14 mm round-topped PETG rail. Catches: at each top corner of each end wall a printed PETG housing (49 mm long, 32 mm tall) holds a 16 x 16 mm thumb button standing 6 mm out of the rail's outer face, 100 mm either side of the wall's middle (200 mm apart). The button is the end of a 13 mm slide (3.8 g) on a Lee Spring LC 024C 08M compression spring (1.278 N/mm, fitted with 2.15 mm preload): 2.7 N at rest, 7.2 N pressed in 3.5 mm, 10.4 N pressed flush (6 mm). A 45 degree cam on the slide pulls an 8 x 3 mm tongue in as far as the button goes in. At rest the tongue stands 4 mm out of the wall's side edge and 3 mm deep into a slot in a 4 mm keeper on the long wall's inner face, so a corner is free once its button is in 3.5 mm. An end wall tips in only while both its corners are free; tipped past 7.4 degrees its tongues are past the keepers, and it folds down onto its rim. A long wall's ends bear on any end wall still standing, so it folds only once both end walls are down; pushed in over its stop it then folds down on top of them. Folded flat the crate is 80 mm tall. The crate slides on the table at about 3.5 N. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Followed over the whole trial: 0 for good if the crate falls off the table (its base more than 10 cm below the table top) or if a catch is forced, that is a latched end wall, or a long wall held up by a latched end wall, is pushed in more than 3 degrees (about 30 N at its top rail). Judged at the end, on live states, a wall lies flat when it is within 5 degrees of its folded stop. 1.0: all four walls flat with the long walls over the flat end walls, the folded crate under 90 mm tall at its highest point, its base on the table and within 3 degrees of level, and both arms back where they started (each gripper's fingertip centre within 5 cm of its start). Otherwise 0.2 for each end wall lying flat plus 0.2 for each long wall lying flat over both flat end walls, at most 0.8. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the crate and its walls still. In a real trial: measure the folded height with a ruler (under 90 mm); check from the video that the crate stayed on the table, that each wall ended lying on its flat stop, and that the long walls lie over the end walls; check the arms against tape marks at their start. A forced catch is judged by inspection after the trial: stand each end wall back up; both its catches must click in, and no tongue may be bent or cracked and no keeper cracked or whitened. Any such damage, or a catch that no longer engages, scores 0. The built catch is rigid, so a latched wall cannot be pushed in without damaging a catch; the simulation's latch gives slightly and flags a push past 3 degrees, about 30 N, which is stricter.
reset_notes: Lift each long wall up onto its stop, then swing each end wall up until both its catches click. Check that all four catches engage and are undamaged. Put the erect crate back centred at (0.23, 0.00), its length along x.
fidelity: Rigid bodies in Isaac Sim (PhysX, 240 Hz) at the built crate's sizes, masses and centres of mass; buttons on sprung slides with the specified spring's rate and preload. Simplified: a stiff hinge spring (1.2 N m per degree) stands in for each end wall's tongues and keepers and lets go while both its buttons are in 3.5 mm or more; cams, tongues, hinge leaves, rail tabs and screws are not modelled. Walls are solid plates of the panels' outer size. PP friction 0.35.
